---
title: "Build a data pipeline"
subtitle: "Filter, sort and join two datasets end to end"
---

This tutorial builds a small analytics pipeline over two related datasets —
employees and the departments they belong to. Along the way you'll use array
construction, compute kernels, row filtering, sorting and a hash join. Every
cell runs when the docs are built.

```{python}
#| echo: false
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "../../python")   # the built extension
import marrow as ma
from marrow import compute as mc
```

## The data

We start with two `RecordBatch`es. The first holds employees; the second maps
department ids to names.

```{python}
employees = ma.record_batch({
    "name":    ma.array(["Alice", "Bob", "Carol", "Dave", "Eve", "Frank"]),
    "dept_id": ma.array([1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 1]),
    "salary":  ma.array([95_000, 72_000, 120_000, 88_000, 61_000, 105_000]),
    "age":     ma.array([34, 28, 45, 52, 24, 39]),
})

departments = ma.record_batch({
    "dept_id": ma.array([1, 2, 3]),
    "dept":    ma.array(["Engineering", "Sales", "Marketing"]),
})

print(employees)
print(departments)
```

## Step 1 — filter rows

Filtering *rows* has two spellings, and it is worth seeing both.

The **query layer** is the one you will reach for. `col(...)` names a column,
comparison operators build a predicate, and the engine applies it to every
column for you:

```{python}
from marrow import col, lit

top_earners = (
    ma.memtable(employees)
      .filter(col("salary") > lit(80_000))
      .collect()
)
print(top_earners.to_pylist())
```

The **eager kernels** work a column at a time, so the same thing by hand is a
mask plus a `filter` per column. Reach for this when you already hold a mask:

```{python}
threshold = ma.array([80_000] * employees.num_rows())
well_paid = mc.greater(employees.column("salary"), threshold)
print("mask:", well_paid)

kept = mc.filter(employees.column("name"), well_paid)
print("names:", kept)
```

Note the comparison needs both operands to share a dtype — hence the array of
thresholds. The query layer handles that for you, which is most of why it is
the shorter spelling.

## Step 2 — sort

`sort_by` orders a batch by one or more keys. Pass a list of
`(column, "ascending" | "descending")` tuples; the second argument controls
null placement (`None` uses the default). Multi-column keys are honoured —
ties on the first key break on the next:

```{python}
by_salary = top_earners.sort_by([("dept_id", "ascending"), ("salary", "descending")])
print(by_salary.to_pylist())
```

## Step 3 — join

`join` performs a hash join between two record batches on named key columns.
The signature is
`join(right, keys, right_keys=None, join_type="inner", num_threads=0)`:

- `keys` — list of left-side key column names,
- `right_keys` — right-side names, or `None` to reuse `keys`,
- `join_type` — `"inner"`, `"left"`, `"right"`, `"full"`, `"semi"` or `"anti"`,
- `num_threads` — `0` auto-selects cores, `1` forces the serial path.

Enrich each employee with their department name:

```{python}
enriched = employees.join(departments, ["dept_id"], join_type="inner")
print(enriched.to_pylist())
```

Columns that collide between the two sides are suffixed with `_right`, matching
PyArrow's behaviour.

## Step 4 — put it together

The whole pipeline reads as a short sequence of transformations: join, filter,
sort, project.

```{python}
# 1. join employees to their departments
joined = employees.join(departments, ["dept_id"], join_type="inner")

# 2-4. filter, sort and project as one plan
report = (
    ma.memtable(joined)
      .filter(col("salary") > lit(80_000))
      .order_by(("salary", "descending"))
      .select("name", "dept", "salary")
      .collect()
)
print(report.to_pylist())
```

Only the join is eager here — it is a `RecordBatch` method. Everything after it
is one plan, so the engine sees the filter, the sort and the projection
together instead of materializing an intermediate batch per step.

## Step 5 — aggregate

Aggregation is not an eager kernel call — it happens inside a **query plan**.
Wrap the batch with `ma.memtable()` to get a lazy table, describe what you
want, and call `.collect()` to run it. Nulls are skipped:

```{python}
q = ma.memtable(joined)

totals = q.aggregate(
    headcount=("count", "salary"),
    total_spend=("sum", "salary"),
    top_salary=("max", "salary"),
)
print(totals.collect().to_pylist())
```

The same call with a `by=` key groups instead of reducing to one row — one code
path for both:

```{python}
by_dept = (
    q.aggregate(
        by=["dept"],
        headcount=("count", "salary"),
        avg_salary=("mean", "salary"),
    )
    .order_by("dept")
)
print(by_dept.collect().to_pylist())
```

Nothing has run until `.collect()`, so a plan is a reusable template — and
`explain()` shows what will happen:

```{python}
print(by_dept.explain())
```
